name: Fuoco Pizzeria Napoletana
body:
Listed as one of the best pizzas in America by the Washington Post, the pies at Fuoco Pizzeria Napoletana emerge from a nearly 1,000-degree wood-burning oven built in Naples by Stefano Ferrara — producing crusts that are airy, blistered, and char-kissed. Three generations of pizzaiolos continue churning out classic margherita pizzas and the Fuoco pie, which is topped with mozzarella, prosciutto crudo, arugula, and shaved Parmigiano, and drizzled with truffle oil. A mozzarella bar is stocked weekly with cheese imported from Caserta, Italy. The place hums with local pride, and the dining room fills up quickly.

Know before you go: Every Monday you can get a $5 margherita with the purchase of any other pizza.

name: Khan Saab Desi Craft Kitchen
body:
This Michelin-recommended halal restaurant combines the flavors of India, Afghanistan, and Pakistan with a modern Californian twist. The tender boneless chicken karahi is served with tomatoes and shishito peppers, and the butter chicken with dried fenugreek is one of the restaurant’s more popular dishes. The pani puri with tamarind water, mint, onion, and potato arrives on a mini cart and is intended to be taken as a shooter. Expect richly spiced biryani, charred kebabs, and a nonalcoholic cocktail program that holds its own.

Must-try dishes: Smoked beef kabob, chicken karahi, and tandoori jhinga.

name: Adya
body:
Chef Shachi Mehra combines her Jersey roots and Indian heritage to create a tangy goat cheese-filled naan. The RFC sandwich combines flavors of a popular Rajasthani snack, which acts as a coating for crispy fried chicken served inside a custom bun made by Dean Kim’s OC Baking Company. Mehra’s inventiveness garnered her a win on Food Network’s Chopped. Meanwhile, her chef-partner, Sandeep Basrur, combines his background in traditional Indian cooking to prepare classics such as a spiced lamb curry, dal makhni, and chicken biryani.

Know before you go: Parking can be a bit of a challenge, especially during peak hours. There’s a small parking lot, but it fills up quickly. Your best bet is street parking.

name: Al Baraka Restaurant
body:
Aref Shatarah and wife Majeda opened Al Baraka in 2023 specializing in Palestinian dishes; regulars tend to recommend the homestyle daily specials. Start with the sheikh el mahshi, fried squash stuffed with a medley of pine nuts and ground beef cooked in yogurt. The tender chicken and the marinated grape leaves filled with rice, onion, tomato, and verdant herbs set Al Baraka apart in Anaheim’s already vibrant Little Arabia district. It’s the kind of family restaurant that feels warm and familiar — generous, reliable, and portions are sized to feed groups.

Must-try dish: Mansaf, only available on Fridays.

name: Ohshima
body:
In an unassuming Orange strip mall, Ohshima quietly serves some of the county’s most dependable sushi. Whether you go at lunch or dinner, the restaurant feels calm and measured — sushi, sashimi, rolls, plus traditional Japanese entrees like fish collar and grilled beef tongue — all delivered with proper rice seasoning and deft fish preparation. There’s no omakase theater here, no flashy decor — just well-made fish, clean flavors, and simple excellence that keeps regulars coming weekly. Try a cold sake (available by the glass or bottle) with the uni chawamushi.

Must-try dish: Chef’s seasonal fish.

name: Kareem's Falafel
body:
As one of the oldest restaurants in Anaheim’s Little Arabia District, Kareem’s remains a go-to for Middle Eastern food. Owner Kareem Hawari’s closely held family falafel recipe is so popular that the Hawaris started selling it wholesale to grocery stores and other restaurants. The baba ganoush, grape leaves, and hummus are staples not to miss, but Kareem’s newer menu items — vegetarian wraps, falafel sliders, and feta fries — also offer modern takes on dishes without sacrificing traditional flavor. The small restaurant gets packed during the lunch rush, but diners can usually find outdoor patio seating to enjoy a leisurely spread.

Must-try dish: The falafel plate.

name: Katella Bakery, Deli & Restaurant
body:
The family-owned Los Alamitos landmark, founded by Sam Ratman and his wife Shirley, is known for its deli food and stocked bakery case that has black-and-white cookies, pastries such as custard-filled eclairs, chocolate chip Danishes, and rugelach. The family-sized portions allow diners to nosh on several dishes at once. Rotund matzo balls are served in Shirley’s chicken soup and rye bread pastrami sandwiches remain a Katella favorite. The vibe is family-friendly with a multi-generational crowd in the dining room, which was remodeled in 2022. The bakery section has illuminated cases filled with slices of layer cakes, cookies, and glistening fruit tarts, baskets filled with bagels, and a smattering of deli items available for takeaway.

Must-try dishes: Matzo ball soup, pastrami, and everything from the bakery case.

name: Anepalco
body:
Chef Daniel Godinez’s Anepalco is one of the pioneers in Orange County’s modern Mexican dining scene, combining ancestral foodways with modern techniques. The menu, which presents as refined yet familiar, runs the gamut from chilaquiles (legendary since it first opened for its dense disc version of the dish) in smoky guajillo sauce to mole negro enchiladas and mezcal-forward cocktails that make a strong case for lingering. The vibe feels contemporary but not fussy — sleek lines, warm lighting, and plates that look as good as they taste. It’s the kind of restaurant that made locals rethink what Mexican food can mean in Orange County.

Must-try dishes: Mole negro enchiladas, ceviche, and chile relleno.

name: Smoke Queen Barbecue
body:
Smoke Queen Barbecue has established itself in Garden Grove as an Asian-style barbecue joint that isn’t afraid to push beyond the expected. Chef-owner Winnie Yee’s restaurant leans into low-and-slow smoking techniques, turning out brisket, gochujang beef ribs, pork belly char siu, and other smoked meats that are tender, deeply seasoned, and rich with smoke. Smoke Queen stands out for its Chinese and Malaysian flavors, as well as its sauces and sides that add dimension without overpowering the barbecue fundamentals: think mapo chile, house-pickled spicy cucumbers, and coconut rice. The space itself feels relaxed and unfussy — more neighborhood hangout than destination dining room — but the aromas alone signal something serious happening in the smoker. It’s an easy choice for casual dinners or group feasts where ordering family-style is the move.

Insider tip: Arrive earlier in the day if you want your pick of cuts, since favorites often sell out by noon.

name: Mo Ran Gak
body:
Korean barbecue is nothing new in Orange County, but Mo Ran Gak has earned Little Seoul cult status. The Garden Grove flagship has been a pilgrimage site for its naengmyeon — icy buckwheat noodles in beef broth or spicy “bibim” — long before social media caught on. The noodles here get made in-house, each bundle springy and cold enough to shock the palate in the best way. The barbecue setup is classic: generous cuts, heaps of banchan, steamed egg, and the kind of energy that makes a weeknight feel like a celebration. It’s loud, packed, and always worth the wait.

Must-try dish: Naengmyeon.

name: Garlic and Chives
body:
Garlic & Chives is one of those Little Saigon spots that never seems to lose momentum. The Mall of Fortune stalwart offers a variety of Vietnamese comfort dishes with unapologetic flavor — crunchy wings doused in garlic and Sichuan spice, garlic noodles topped with plump black tiger shrimp, fried salmon belly, sizzling cubes of toothpick lamb. This menu may be wide, but its execution is sharp; expect dishes to deliver plenty of its namesake aromatics. Inside, the room hums with energy, plates hit the table fast, and every dish feels built for sharing, especially mains like lamb chops or caramelized catfish with pork belly. There’s little subtlety and that’s part of the joy.

Must-try dishes: Wings, garlic noodles, and toothpick lamb.

name: Banh Cuon Luu Luyen
body:
Lưu Luyến occupies the corner spot of a shopping plaza, which means it has a whole row of parking spots to itself — perfect for the long lines it regularly draws for its bánh cuốn. Delicate steamed rice sheets are spun paper-thin, then stretched, filled, and rolled to order with savory pork, shrimp, or mushrooms. Each plate lands with shards of fried shallots, fragrant herbs, and chile-infused nuoc cham good enough for a mason jar and ladle. Other dishes include spring rolls, bun moc soup, nem heo (fermented pork), but the bánh cuốn are the reason to come. The tiny dining room fills up quickly, so come early or be prepared to wait alongside locals who know exactly why it’s worth it.

Must-try dish: Bánh cuốn.

name: Pho 79
body:
This is not just another pho shop — Phở 79 is the institution. Thọ Trần and Liễu Trần’s restaurant has ladled out hot bowls of steaming pho since 1982. Step in and find a spartan but inviting sunshine-yellow interior adorned with a wall of honors — James Beard America’s Classics award and a Michelin Bib Gourmand being the most prominent. The broth runs deep and fragrant with star anise — a base that can hold brisket, tendon, oxtail, or, ideally, all three. Because the place is so loved, expect waits, but there’s a rhythm to the room that feels like clockwork precision — service is brisk and tables turn fast. Some places get crowded because they’re trendy; this one stays crowded because it’s timeless.

Must-try dish: Oxtail pho with brisket and tendon.

name: Fat Of The Land
body:
Fat of the Land has carved out a thoughtful niche in Santa Ana, appealing to diners drawn to its coastal Spanish tapas, consistency, and attentive care. The menu emphasizes seasonality, resulting in dishes that feel intentional and balanced — octopus carpaccio in a mojo vinaigrette, a rack of pork, and Piquillo peppers stuffed with Iberian pork and fennel slaw — striking a balance between rustic and refined. The dining room mirrors that sensibility: accented with warm brass, dark-wood chairs and ornate mirrors, soft lights hidden in gentle fixtures, textured wallpaper, and a white marble bar. To complement the food, Fat of the Land’s wine list features a regional collection of Spanish wine. This is a place designed for lingering meals, whether for an intimate dinner or a longer catch-up over shared plates.

Must-try dish: Ask about the seasonal specials, which often showcase what the kitchen team is most excited about at the moment.

name: Alta Baja Market
body:
Delilah Snell’s Alta Baja Market is the heart of downtown Santa Ana. It’s also a community pillar: the market received the 2023 Siete Family Foods’ Siete Juntos Fund, which strives to support and empower Latino communities. Alta Baja Market’s breakfast and lunch menu includes dishes such as New Mexican blue cornbread with honey butter and Lady C’s green chile eggchilada, which resembles a breakfast casserole using La Princesita tortillas. The market’s specialty grocery section includes one of the largest selections of Mexican wines in the U.S., along with a variety of heirloom corn, beans, and grains. To get the full experience, order one of Alta Baja’s signature micheladas. La Chiquita, made with passion fruit, is a sweet and spicy complement to any dish.

Know before you go: The last Sunday of every month is “Pozole Sunday.” Snell offers two styles — Zacatecas-style pork pozole rojo and vegan pozole verde from Guerrero — from 10 a.m. until sold out. And they will run out.

name: Omakase by Gino
body:
Sushi chef Gino Choi prepares an intricate omakase for 10 diners at his namesake downtown Santa Ana restaurant. (Choi is also a self-taught carpenter who built the sushi counter, entryway, and partitions himself.) Standout dishes include a creamy Hokkaido uni udon garnished with winter black truffles from Spain; Gino’s version of tamago, flavored with shellfish; and a yuzu foam topped with slow-cooked black cod bedded alongside green plum marinated roasted tomatoes. Choi serves four days a week with two seatings per night; the cost is $250 per person, and reservations vanish fast.

Know before you go: Reservations release on Resy every second Sunday of the month at 10 a.m., so set a timer to secure a spot.

name: Nok’s Kitchen
body:
Chef Nokmaniphone Sayavong’s Laotian food built a cult following with her grilled sausage and tum mak houng, grated papaya salad mixed with tomato and seasoned with fish sauce. The herbaceous pork sausage should be eaten with sticky rice, a Laotian staple, and dipped in tangy, spiced jeow som, interspersed with bites of fresh cucumber. The khao pad, her signature fried rice, comes with either tofu, chicken, pork, shrimp, or crab. Nok’s turns out dishes that balance home-style comfort with restaurant polish. All of this can be had in its dining room with dark walls, rattan fixtures, and a centerpiece mural.

Must-try dish: Lao sausage.

name: Chaak
body:
Chaak Kitchen in Old Town Tustin is the sister restaurant to Gabbi’s Mexican Kitchen in Orange. The food pulls inspiration from Yucatán, Mayan, and European flavors — wood-grilled meats, smoky recados, and masa in all its glorious forms. Starters such as sikil p’ak, a creamy pumpkin seed dip, and mains like the cochinita pibil, achiote-smoked pork shoulder, remain examples of how this lush, modern restaurant, with its retractable roof and ample sidewalk patio dining, pushes the expectations of Mexican food found in Orange County. Don’t skip the wines from Mexico and cocktails from its robust menu.

Must-try dishes: Chuuk trio, cochinita pibil, and tamal colado.

name: Taco Mesita
body:
Taco Mesita has quietly become a locals’ favorite in Tustin. The modern fast-food menu has an Alta California touch and lets quality wood-fired meats and seasonal ingredients do the heavy lifting: think skirt steak tacos served on organic hand-pressed blue corn tortillas, panela taquitos crowned by fresh cheese and avocado crema, and rotisserie pollo burrito filled with a vibrant tomatillo corn cabbage relish. Signature whipped jalapeño salsa adds personality, bringing heat and brightness that punch up each bite. Mesita’s breakfast features just as noteworthy steak or chorizo breakfast tacos, each finished with poblano strips, crispy cheese, potato, pickled onion, and sous vide egg. The space has a compact and warm neutral patio surrounded by lush landscaping, with a steady stream of locals cycling through the drive-thru — always a good sign.

Know before you go: Late-night happy hour is from 9 p.m. to close every day, which includes $2 margaritas and $3 pork shoulder tacos.

name: Brodard Restaurant
body:
This landmark restaurant offers a wide array of Vietnamese specialties, starting with 13 types of spring rolls — including its signature, nem nuong cuon. Grilled pork with lettuce, carrots, a slender piece of deep-fried egg-roll skin, mint, chives, and cucumber wrapped in rice paper. The menu continues with traditional Vietnamese noodle soups, rice porridge packed with sole, and banh xeo crepe filled with shrimp, sliced pork, mung beans, sprouts and a mountain of herbs..The dining room gleams — lively, family-driven, and full of laughter over shared plates.

Must-try dish: Nem nuong cuon.

name: Mariscos El Yaqui
body:
Once a humble Baja California-style lonchera, El Yaqui now anchors its own standalone space in Santa Ana — and the seafood remains the draw. The counters are simple and the plates generous: think ceviche towers, shrimp or fish tacos (fried or grilled), smoky marlin, and butterflied raw shrimp aguachile platters with lots of lime. Look for the Pokastrankas stack — a mountain of seafood, avocado, and serrano heat that regulars swear by. What you won’t get anywhere else is the cahuamanta, a spicy soup made with shrimp and manta ray, an invigorating pottage that has its roots in caguama (Mexican sea-turtle soup that became outlawed once the species became endangered). El Yaqui’s cahuamanta doesn’t skimp on the manta, whose flavor is similar to that of squid. If you order correctly, you’ll leave smelling like lime, and that’s precisely the point.

Must-try dish: Cahuamanta.

name: Nep Cafe
body:
Nep Cafe is a brunch sensation. At the French Vietnamese all-day cafe, run by the massively successful restaurant group Kei Concepts, the kitchen pays “homage to the traditional Vietnamese morning routine.” The menu includes TikTok-worthy coffee drinks topped with salted egg yolk and delicate dishes like curry crab omelet. Nep’s second location in Irvine opened in the same plaza as Kei Concepts’ Sup Noodle Bar. It’s perpetually packed, and the iced coffee is strong enough to rewrite your morning.

Must-try: Egg coffee, crab toast, and crispy pork rice bowl.

name: The Parlor
body:
Tucked inside a quiet plaza, chef Jimmy Stafford’s Parlor restaurant turns out fresh pastas like rigatoni Bolognese, bucatini all’Amatriciana, sausage and rapini paccheri, and rosemary focaccia worthy of its own Netflix special. Pizzas come from a wood-fired oven, their edges blistered and charred just enough — the Fiori e Limone with dollops of stracciatella, zucchini, Meyer lemon, and a hit of brightness might be the sleeper pick of the year. The space leans casual-industrial with counter-order service, making it the kind of weekday haunt that’s easy to drop into for takeout or a laid-back dinner. Weekends are closed (for now), but the word is building fast.

Must-try dishes: Fiori e Limone pizza and whatever il panino they have on special.

name: Vaca
body:
Top Chef: All Stars’ Amar Santana opened this sleek Spanish hideaway in 2016 inside the Segerstrom Performing Arts Center. Aged steaks hang from illuminated cases as if perched in a sleek showroom. For friends and family, a specially priced menu only available on Mondays, the wagyu and bone marrow burger gets punched up with Fiscalini cheddar, crisp cabbage, and truffle aioli. Those looking for paella will find options with saffron-hinted bomba rice. But the sharable tapas are the most fun. The chef’s snacks rotate often, but the creamy chicken croquettes and warm pulpo with fingerling potatoes drizzled in Spanish olive oil remain mainstays since it opened.

Know before you go: Every Monday is Friends and Family, which offers a specially priced menu.

name: Knife Pleat
body:
This modern French-Californian restaurant from chef Tony Esnault and Yassmin Sarmadi is ripe for celebratory meals. The three-course lunch and four-to-six-course dinner prix fixe menus change often. One week, it’s French black truffles; another evening, it’s a Nowruz dinner with recipes by Shamsi Katebi, prepared by Esnault and his kitchen team. Its plush banquets and round tables overlook the bar and open kitchen. A sunlit patio is typically booked with private weekend events, and a pricey but impeccable afternoon tea service is available on Saturdays. The surprisingly satisfying non-alcoholic cocktails, like the Cadillac margarita with orange, pomegranate, and lime, are also worth stopping in for.

Must-try: The Collection.

name: Yigah
body:
Korean comfort food served in large portions is what Yigah is known for in Orange County. The restaurant located within the Diamond Jamboree shopping center serves steamy galbi tang, beef short rib soup, as well as the bossam meal with boiled pork belly, napa cabbage, and spicy pickled radish. The soups — especially the spicy beef or ox knee varieties — arrive steaming and full of depth, while crisp tonkatsu and sizzling hot-stone bibimbap round out the soul-warming lineup. The room is as casual as it gets, the kind of place you can turn to on cold nights and quiet weekends.

Must-try dish: Spicy beef soup and bibimbap.

name: A&J Restaurant
body:
This Taiwanese restaurant in Irvine serves Chinese-style crispy pork chop over rice and thousand-layer pancakes, but the noodle dishes are not to be missed, including a beef noodle soup with deep peppery broth and noodles with ground pork. For diners who enjoy heat, the menu also features several Sichuan-style dishes, like beef tendon with garlic sauce and spicy wontons with a hint of sweetness and heat that doesn’t overpower. Pair it with a Chinese beef wrap or dumplings and you’ll understand why this shop is always full. It’s fast, warm, and feels like a familiar memory even the first time you visit.

Must-try dishes: Beef noodle soup, pan-fried beef bun, and spicy wontons.

name: Hana re
body:
The omakase-only Hana re is a 10-seat sushi-ya helmed by Atsushi Yokoyama. Located in an industrial storage crate at the Lab in Costa Mesa, the counter, which held a Michelin star from 2019 to 2024, feels like a hidden gem, even though its stellar fish preparations are no secret anymore. Yokoyama and one server, who also assists with wine pairings, put out an omakase experience that includes bite-sized crab perched atop eel tempura, scallops enveloped in gelee, Whelk shellfish with celery root, caviar, and shiso. Reservations can be made via text at (714) 545-2800 for the $250 omakase.

Know before you go: Four guests are the maximum number for each party.

name: Mario's Butcher Shop
body:
The strip mall butcher shop and deli serves pastrami sandwiches layered with beef cured in-house on rye bread. The rotating specials board includes fish and chips, and Texas cheese and porchetta sandwiches. The smash burger made with beef ground in-house and the Italian sub — that incorporates a combination of Genoa, coppa, soppressata, and Parmesan — remain the favorites for regulars. You can grab a sandwich stacked with prime rib or sit down to a steak cut that was probably trimmed an hour ago. The generously stocked shop sells an impressive variety of cheeses, homemade salads, olive oil, charcuterie, and other gourmet foods.

Must-try dishes: Smash burger, pastrami sandwich, and smoked bologna.

name: Hook and Anchor
body:
For first-timers, the lobster roll and creamy clam chowder at this seafood spot are a gateway experience. Bites of the buttery toasted bun stuffed with succulent claw meat get interspersed with slurps of homemade chowder with whole baby clams — the dish evokes memories of the best old-school seafood houses. Venture beyond the lobster roll: The rest of the menu includes favorites like crispy tempura-battered mahi mahi fish and chips, as well as wild-caught seafood for surf-and-turf plates. In June, it opened a second location along a popular stretch of La Plaza in Dana Point.

Must-try dish: Lobster roll with a side of Parmesan fries.

name: A Restaurant
body:
This cozy red booth hideout on Pacific Coast Highway is known for its Rat Pack atmosphere. The classic martini reigns at the bar, and the chicken pot pie is only available on Monday and Friday, but locals love the steaks, the roasted Mary’s organic chicken, and pan-seared Niman Ranch pork chops. Put simply: The restaurant is old-school done right. River Jetty Restaurant Group also operates A Restaurant’s sister locales CDM Restaurant, A Crystal Cove, and A Market, which are go-to hot spots in Newport Beach.

Must-try dishes: Chicken pot pie, Niman Ranch pork belly tacos, and bone-in rib-eye.

name: Fable & Spirit
body:
A meal at Fable & Spirit, almost by default, starts with warm Guinness brown bread with European butter and Jacobsen sea salt. From there, the Lido Isle restaurant weaves between European meat and potato influences to pure California cuisine, like citrusy salads loaded with cara cara and blood oranges, chevre, and crispy quinoa. The fish and chips, lightly battered with a crisp outer layer gives way to pillowy, flaky meat. Fable serves it with vibrant crushed peas, hand-cut fries, and a curry remoulade sauce. The cocktails are inventive; the room lively with emerald green walls, gold accents, and art that plays into the rich mythology of Irish culture. Chef David Shofner and the Coyle family are also known for popular Mission Viejo restaurants Wineworks for Everyone and Dublin 4 Gastropub.

Must-try dish: Fish and chips in the “Snug” booth.

name: Farmhouse at Roger's Gardens
body:
Chef Richard Mead is a long-standing figure in the Orange County dining scene. At the Farmhouse at Roger’s Gardens, the chef showcases the best that the season has to offer from the region’s many producers, which means ever-changing takes on dishes like sea scallops, as well as shrimp and mussels served in a tomato-Pernod broth with a polenta cake made from cornmeal sourced from the Tehachapi Heritage Grain Project. Surrounded by greenery, this open-air restaurant channels farm-to-table sincerity with California ease.

Must-try dishes: Farmhouse market salad and braised green enchiladas.

name: Marché Moderne
body:
Florent and Amelia Marneu’s white tablecloth restaurant is a stalwart in the Orange County fine dining scene. The Newport Beach restaurant serves traditional French favorites such as roasted chicken cordon bleu and duck confit. Amelia’s chopped salad with French feta, cucumber, mint, and honey grapefruit vinaigrette showcases California produce. Other standout dishes include hamachi with a jalapeño-tinged mango-yuzu sorbet, grilled octopus with chorizo, and the rotating desserts dreamed up by the Marneus.

Must-try dishes: Chef’s tasting menu, available Wednesday to Sunday.

name: Selanne Steak Tavern
body:
Laguna Beach locals love this place for its white tablecloths, award-winning wine program, and stellar steaks. The vibrant golden beetravioli stuffed with goat cheese is a striking starter, while a delicate souffle finishes the meal. Former Anaheim Ducks hockey player and six-time Olympian Teemu Selanne is one of the restaurant’s owners, so be on the lookout for Orange County A-listers. Prime cuts, rich sauces, and a deep cellar of wines define the experience, while the converted 1930s home gives it character. It’s a place for celebrations, proposals, or just unapologetically indulgent evenings by the coast.

Must-try dishes: Lord Stanley for two guests, Parmesan truffle risotto, and scarlet beet “ravioli.”

name: Heritage Barbecue
body:
The line outside Heritage Barbecue says it all. San Juan Capistrano’s award-winning pitmaster Daniel Castillo — a 2025 James Beard Award finalist for Best Chef: California — takes barbecue to the next level with wood-smoked brisket with deep bark, sausages, turkey, ribs that fall clean off the bone, herb-seasoned chicken, and more. First-timers load up on the brisket and ribs, while regulars order sandwich specials like the tip French dip, brisket tacos prepared with La Palma tortillas, and creamy banana pudding layered with pound cake and vanilla wafer cookies. Get the charred broccoli with cheesy mornay sauce if it’s on the menu.

Know before you go: They are open until “sell out” meaning their closing hour will change day-to-day. Your best bet is to come early.

name: Mayfield
body:
George Barker opened Mayfield in 2020 and sparked a new dining movement in San Juan Capistrano. The food is influenced by Levantine regional flavors, with hints of North Africa, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East mixed with classic Californian approaches. Find a solid burger with harissa aioli at happy hour and za’atar fried chicken for dinner. For brunch, there’s avocado toast and egg sandwiches, but there are also Turkish eggs with labneh and fiery tomato shakshuka, showcasing the variety from the kitchen. The restaurant is also known for its cocktails: sip on a papa picante topped with habanero bitters or a well-made Negroni.

Must-try dishes: Za’atar fried chicken, cauliflower shawarma, and shakshuka.

name: Truly Pizza
body:
This partnership from chef Chris Decker, Michael Vakneen, Donna Baldwin, and John Arena brings some of the best pizza in Southern California to Dana Point. Hearth-baked 12-inch American artisan pizzas like The Dante with vodka sauce, provola, chicken sausage, and pickled peppers emerge from the kitchen. But the coveted square pizzas combine the fluffy chew of focaccia with a quintessential cheese pull. The classic pepperoni is slathered with a nuanced California red sauce and topped with fresh and aged whole milk mozzarella and charred pepperoni. Save space for Strauss Creamery organic vanilla soft serve with drizzles of chocolate sauce or flecks of pistachio.

Must-try dishes: The Dante, smoky vodka, and garlic pull-apart bread.
